client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed thinking about my final exams next month. I barely passed chemistry last semester, and now I keep imagining myself failing again no matter how much I study. Part of me wonders if talking about it will actually help, since the exams are coming no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of worry about these exams, especially with your past experience in chemistry making the anxiety feel more real. I notice your voice speeds up when talking about failing no matter how much you study—that tells me this is really weighing on you. Would it help to explore what makes this particular exam feel different from ones you've prepared for successfully before?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess what makes this different is that last semester I barely passed chemistry, and now I'm terrified of falling behind again. No matter how much I study, I keep imagining the worst-case scenario where I completely blank out during the test. It feels like my brain just shuts down when I'm actually in the exam room.
therapist: Your voice gets quieter and faster when describing that moment of blanking out—it seems like you're reliving that panic just talking about it. Let's slow down for a moment: what usually happens right *before* your brain shuts down in those exam situations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I can feel my hands getting clammy just thinking about it. Right before my mind goes blank, I start noticing everyone else writing furiously and I think "I'm falling behind already." But when you say to slow down, it's like... how? The clock's still ticking and my chest feels tight.
therapist: I hear how physically intense this experience is for you—the clammy hands, the tight chest, the racing thoughts about others' progress. That moment when you notice yourself comparing to others seems like a key trigger point. What would happen if you tried a grounding technique right then, like feeling your feet on the floor, before the panic spirals?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get why you're suggesting grounding, but when I'm in that moment of comparing myself to others, it feels impossible to focus on my feet. My mind just races with thoughts like "Why can't I keep up?" and "They must think I'm failing." It's like my body and thoughts are moving too fast to control.
therapist: It sounds like in those moments, the self-critical thoughts become so loud that they drown out everything else, including helpful strategies. Let's try something different—what if we worked on catching and challenging those "why can't I keep up" thoughts before they gain momentum?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but when those thoughts come up, they feel so true in the moment. Like, I'll see coworkers finishing tasks faster and immediately think "of course you're falling behind again." It's hard to even recognize it's happening until I'm already spiraling.
therapist: I notice your voice softens when describing these moments—it seems like you're observing this pattern with more clarity now, even though the thoughts still feel true in the moment. That awareness is actually the first step toward change. Would you be willing to try naming those automatic thoughts out loud when they happen, like "Ah, there's my 'falling behind' thought again"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but I'm not sure naming the thoughts will help. When I'm in that anxious spiral, it feels so overwhelming that just labeling it seems too simple. Plus, sometimes saying it out loud makes the thought feel even more real and scary to me.
therapist: It makes complete sense that naming the thoughts feels too simple when the anxiety is at its peak—like trying to stop a wave with your hands. I hear you're also worried that acknowledging the thoughts might amplify them, which is a very common concern. Would it feel safer to start by noticing these patterns after they happen, rather than in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, slow speech

client:
Yeah, I guess looking back at the anxious thoughts after they happen might feel less overwhelming. But sometimes even remembering them later makes me feel that same panic all over again. I worry that focusing on it at all just keeps the cycle going. 

I see what you're saying about it being like trying to stop a wave, because that's exactly how it feels - completely out of control. But I'm not sure if looking backward will help when the problem is how it feels in the moment.
therapist: Your voice speeds up when describing how remembering brings back that panic—it's clear this cycle feels relentless to you. You're absolutely right that we don't want to reinforce the pattern, so let's think together about what kind of reflection might feel helpful rather than re-triggering. Would writing down the thoughts (rather than saying them aloud) create enough distance to observe them without getting pulled back in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know if writing would help...when I try to put the thoughts on paper, they just feel more real and permanent somehow. Like if I write it down, then it's proof that I really am this messed up. But I do see what you mean about getting pulled back in - that happens every time I try to talk about it too.
therapist: I hear that sense of permanence when you write things down—like the words might cement those painful thoughts rather than help you work through them. Your voice rises when talking about feeling "messed up," showing how deeply this belief affects you. What if we tried a different approach—maybe drawing the anxious thoughts instead of writing them, to create some symbolic distance?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Drawing them? I don't know...I'm not artistic at all. I feel like my terrible drawings would just make me feel worse about myself. And wouldn't that still keep me stuck on the same negative thoughts, just in picture form? 

I guess I'm worried this is another thing I'll fail at, like how I feel like I'm failing at just being normal. Writing at least feels familiar, even if it makes me spiral sometimes.
therapist: Your voice gets higher and quicker when talking about failing at being "normal"—that tells me how much this belief is weighing on you. Let's set aside the drawing idea for now, since it seems to be bringing up those familiar fears of not measuring up. You mentioned writing feels familiar—what if we tried adjusting that approach slightly, like tearing up the paper afterward as a symbolic way to let go of those thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
Tearing up the paper... I don't know, that kinda feels like just pretending the thoughts aren't there. Like if I write down "I'm a failure" and then rip it up, the thought's still in my head, you know? It's not that simple. 

The writing part might help though. When I journal sometimes, it does make the anxious thoughts feel less overwhelming. But then I always end up rereading it later and feeling worse about myself.
therapist: It sounds like you've found a middle ground with journaling—it helps in the moment but gets complicated when you revisit it later. That makes perfect sense, since our relationship with our own thoughts often changes over time. What if we experimented with writing followed by something to mark closure, like putting the pages away in a special folder rather than rereading them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
